tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

content.text:
I checked the environment before planning anything. Three things came up before any code:

- **The git repo is rooted at your home folder (`C:/Users/Samitha`), not this project.** `ticket_stampede` is just a subfolder of a repo that also sees `.ssh/`, `.aws/` and `NTUSER.DAT`. If anything ever ran `git add .` from home and pushed, those would leak. I recommend running `git init` inside `ticket_stampede` so the project has its own repo. The git history will also be part of your evidence.
- **Docker Desktop isn't running.** The CLI is there (Compose v5.0.1), but the engine isn't. Please start it before we run anything.
- **The project folder is empty**, apart from `.claude/`. Python 3.12.4 is available.

---

## Milestone 1: naive seller

**What it's for:** a seller that is broken in a realistic, explainable way, so the load client can catch the failure later. It is not the goal itself.

**What the naive `/buy` does** (plain autocommit, no transaction, no lock):
1. `SELECT` the ticket row for this `request_id`. If one exists, return it. This is a check-then-act race on idempotency.
2. Read how many tickets are sold, and return sold-out if that's at or above the total.
3. Wait `NAIVE_DELAY_MS`.
4. `INSERT` a ticket with `ticket_number = sold + 1`. This is a check-then-act race on capacity and uniqueness.

### The honesty question: is the delay rigging the test?
My position: the race exists without the delay, and the delay only widens the window so the failure is reproducible on a laptop. The delay stands in for real work between check and write, like a payment call or a slow network hop. We shouldn't just claim that, though. We should show it: run the naive seller with `NAIVE_DELAY_MS=0` as well, and report whatever happens. If it still oversells at 0 ms, that's strong evidence. If it doesn't, we say so and explain why the window is small. An interviewer will almost certainly ask "didn't you just add a sleep to make it break?", so you want real numbers from both runs.

### Files I'd create (please approve)
```
ticket_stampede/
  docker-compose.yml        # postgres:16 + seller
  seller/Dockerfile
  seller/requirements.txt   # fastapi, uvicorn, asyncpg
  seller/app.py             # /reset, /buy (naive), /status
  seller/schema_naive.sql   # tables with NO constraints
  DECISIONS_LOG.md          # running decision log (becomes DECISIONS.md)
```
Nothing for the load client yet; that's Milestone 2.

---

## Decisions I need from you

**1. Database driver**

| Option | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| **asyncpg + raw SQL** (my recommendation) | Every statement and transaction boundary is visible in your own code. When you're asked "where exactly does the transaction start?", you point at a line. |
| SQLAlchemy async ORM | Less SQL to write, but it hides when it opens transactions and flushes writes. That's hard to defend live. |
| psycopg3 | Just as explicit as asyncpg and has a sync mode. Slightly less common with FastAPI. |

**2. Does the naive seller keep a separate `sold` counter?** Think about this one yourself first. Here's the prompt:

> Invariant 4 says `/status`'s count must match the tickets actually issued. If `/status` computes the count as `COUNT(*)` over the tickets table, **can invariant 4 ever fail?**

Once you've answered that, choose:
- **(a)** The naive seller stores `sold` on the `sale` row and updates it with read-modify-write, which many real systems do for fast status reads. Lost updates then produce real drift, so the failing run can show all four invariants breaking.
- **(b)** The seller has no counter and the count is derived from the rows. Invariant 4 then holds by design, and the write-up explains why.

Both are honest. They tell different stories.

**3. What shape does `/status` return?** This is a subtle trap worth thinking about. The spec says it returns "the mapping of ticket_number → user_id". Suppose we return a JSON object like `{"1": "alice", "2": "bob"}` and the naive seller issues ticket 7 twice. **What happens to that duplicate on the way to the client?** Tell me your answer and we'll use it to decide between returning a JSON object and a list of `{ticket_number, user_id}` pairs.

**4. Minor, with a default unless you object:** sold-out returns HTTP `409` with `{"sold_out": true}`.

---

### Decision log (started)
| # | Decision | Status | Rationale / evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| D0 | Project gets its own git repo | proposed | The repo at home would expose `.ssh`, `.aws` and more |
| D1 | Postgres over in-process lock | accepted (your call) | A process lock doesn't cover multiple instances. Needs evidence in the Milestone 8 multi-instance test |
| D2 | Naive delay is configurable, and the 0 ms run is also reported | proposed | Answers "did you rig it?" with data |
| D3 | Driver | **open** | |
| D4 | Separate `sold` counter in the naive seller | **open** | |
| D5 | `/status` response shape | **open** | |

**Interview flag:** questions 2 and 3 are exactly the kind of thing a live interviewer probes. "Your status endpoint says 100 sold. How do you know that's true?" is the invariant-4 question in disguise.

Once you've answered the four decisions, approved `git init`, and started Docker, I'll write Milestone 1.

The repo is now rooted in the project and Docker is up.

## Milestone 1 design, before writing any files

### Schema (`schema_naive.sql`): deliberately has no constraints
```sql
sale(total_tickets INT, sold_count INT)                  -- single row, no PK
tickets(ticket_number INT, user_id TEXT, request_id TEXT) -- no PK, no UNIQUE
```
The database will accept duplicate `ticket_number`s, duplicate `request_id`s and any number of rows. Every invariant is left to application logic, which is the naive part.

### `/reset {tickets: N}`
Runs the schema file (`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` then `CREATE`), then inserts the sale row. Recreating the tables instead of just truncating them means a later schema change takes effect on reset, with no stale volume state. Reset never runs under load, so the cost doesn't matter.

### `/buy {user_id, request_id}`: autocommit, so each statement is its own transaction
```
1. SELECT ticket_number FROM tickets WHERE request_id=$1   → found? return it   [race A: idempotency]
2. SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale              → sold >= total? 409 [race B: capacity]
3. sleep(NAIVE_DELAY_MS)                                   ← widens the window between check and act
4. INSERT tickets (sold_count+1, ...)                      [race C: two readers of sold=k both write k+1]
5. UPDATE sale SET sold_count = <value read in step 2> + 1 [race D: lost update → drift]
```
Step 5 writes back a value computed in Python, not `sold_count + 1` computed in SQL. That's the classic read-modify-write lost update. If 20 requests all read `sold=5`, you get 20 rows but `sold_count=6`. The low counter then lets even more buyers through step 2, so drift makes the oversell worse too. Interview flag: that feedback loop is worth being able to explain.

### `/status`
Returns `{total_tickets, sold, tickets: [{ticket_number, user_id}, ...]}`. `sold` comes from `sold_count` (D4a), and `tickets` is a list (D5). The two reads aren't a consistent snapshot. That's fine for the naive seller, but I've added it to the log so we come back to it in the corrected one.

### Two things that affect the experiment, not just the code
- **Connection pool size (`DB_POOL_SIZE`, default 10):** a request holds a connection during the delay, so at most 10 requests are in the race window at once. The concurrency the database sees is the pool size, not the 50,000 clients. That matters a lot in Milestone 7.
- **Single uvicorn worker:** one process on purpose. Multiple workers would already make this a multi-instance system, which is the stretch problem, not this one.

import asyncio
import os
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

DATABASE_URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]
DB_POOL_SIZE = int(os.environ.get("DB_POOL_SIZE", "10"))
NAIVE_DELAY_MS = int(os.environ.get("NAIVE_DELAY_MS", "50"))
SCHEMA = (Path(__file__).parent / "schema_naive.sql").read_text()

app = FastAPI()
pool: asyncpg.Pool


@app.on_event("startup")
async def startup():
    global pool
    pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(DATABASE_URL, min_size=DB_POOL_SIZE, max_size=DB_POOL_SIZE)


class ResetRequest(BaseModel):
    tickets: int


class BuyRequest(BaseModel):

content.text:
Milestone 1 is done: the naive seller is running in Docker and passes a one-request-at-a-time smoke test.

**What I added**
- [docker-compose.yml](docker-compose.yml) starts Postgres 16 and the seller, and waits for the database to be ready before starting the seller.
- [seller/schema_naive.sql](seller/schema_naive.sql) creates two tables with no constraints at all.
- [seller/app.py](seller/app.py) has the three endpoints. The naive `/buy` does five separate database steps with no transaction and no lock, plus the configurable delay.
- [seller/Dockerfile](seller/Dockerfile) runs a single uvicorn worker.
- [seller/requirements.txt](seller/requirements.txt) lists the Python dependencies.
- [DECISIONS_LOG.md](DECISIONS_LOG.md) records D0–D8, the smoke-test result, and three open questions.

**Smoke test results:** a replayed `request_id` got the same ticket (`1`), the third buyer got `409 {"sold_out":true}`, and `/status` showed `sold:2` with 2 rows. Concurrent correctness hasn't been tested yet; that's Milestone 2.

**New open question:** what should happen when the same `request_id` arrives with a *different* `user_id`? We don't need an answer yet, but the corrected seller will need one.

### Before Milestone 2: predict what will break
Write this down before we run anything. Take 200 concurrent buyers, 100 tickets, 50 ms delay and a pool of 10 connections:
1. Which of the four invariants will fail?

Committed as `0ba0c9d`. The LF→CRLF warnings come from Git's Windows line-ending setting. They're harmless for Python, SQL and the Dockerfile. If we add shell scripts later we'll need a `.gitattributes` forcing LF, because a `.sh` file with CRLF line endings breaks inside Linux containers. I've noted it for later.

---

## Milestone 2: load client v1

**Scope:** fire concurrent `/buy` requests, replay duplicate `request_id`s, read `/status` afterwards, and check the four invariants with a pass/fail result for each. Latency percentiles, throughput and the cross-check of what clients received against `/status` are **Milestone 6**, so they're deliberately left out here.

**Files:** `buyer/buyer.py` and `buyer/requirements.txt` (`httpx`). The client runs on the host, not in Docker. Only correctness matters in this milestone, and running it outside the seller's containers keeps it clearly separate from the system under test.

### Design choices, with my reasoning

**1. How concurrency is controlled.** The client builds a list of `--requests` jobs up front, and an `asyncio.Semaphore(--concurrency)` caps how many are in flight. **Interview flag:** `httpx.AsyncClient` allows at most 100 connections by default. If `--concurrency 500` ran on that default, the client would quietly send only 100 at a time, and we'd be measuring the client's limit, not the server's. I set the httpx limits from `--concurrency` explicitly.

**2. How duplicates are generated.** `--dup-fraction 0.2` means 20% of request_ids get sent `--dup-copies` times (default 2). Each unique request gets its own `user_id`. That one-to-one link is what lets the client check idempotency against the server's own data, as described in point 3. Copies are placed **next to each other** in the send order, so they're in flight together. That's the case that matters: a client times out and retries while the original is still being processed. A replay sent after the original finished would pass even the naive seller, and the write-up should say we tested the harder case.

**3. How each invariant is checked, and against which data source:**

| Invariant | Check | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1. No oversell | `len(tickets) <= total_tickets` | `/status` rows |
| 2. No duplicate ticket | every `ticket_number` is unique, and in `1..total` | `/status` rows |
| 3. Idempotency | (a) no `user_id` appears in more than one row, since one user equals one request_id; (b) every copy of a request_id got the same ticket_number | (a) `/status` rows; (b) client responses |
| 4. No drift | `sold == len(tickets)` | `/status` counter compared with its own rows |

Idempotency gets two independent checks. (a) catches duplicate rows the server stored. (b) catches a buyer being told two different numbers.

**4. Errors are reported, never hidden.** Status codes other than 200 or 409, and transport exceptions, are counted and printed. A run where 30% of requests failed isn't a valid "pass", so any errors mark the run as **INCONCLUSIVE**.

**How I'll test the client itself in this milestone:** with `--concurrency 1`, the naive seller is correct, so the checker must report **all PASS**. That shows it doesn't produce false alarms. Showing that it catches real failures is Milestone 3's job. I'll stop there.

"""Load client v1: stampede the seller, then check the four invariants."""
import argparse
import asyncio
import random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

import httpx


def build_jobs(n_requests, dup_fraction, dup_copies, seed):
    """Return a send order of (user_id, request_id). Duplicate copies sit adjacent
    so they are in flight at the same time (the retry-while-original-pending case)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    jobs, i = [], 0
    while len(jobs) < n_requests:
        user_id, request_id = f"user-{i}", f"req-{i}"
        copies = dup_copies if rng.random() < dup_fraction else 1
        jobs.extend([(user_id, request_id)] * copies)
        i += 1
    return jobs[:n_requests]


async def run(args):
    jobs = build_jobs(args.requests, args.dup_fraction, args.dup_copies, args.seed)
    limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=args.concurrency, max_keepalive_connections=args.concurrency)
    responses = defaultdict(list)          # request_id -> [ticket_number, ...] from 200s
    codes, errors = Counter(), Counter()
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(args.concurrency)

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=args.url, limits=limits, timeout=args.timeout) as client:
        r = await client.post("/reset", json={"tickets": args.tickets})
        r.raise_for_status()

        async def buy(user_id, request_id):
            async with sem:
                try:
                    r = await client.post("/buy", json={"user_id": user_id, "request_id": request_id})
                except httpx.HTTPError as e:
                    errors[type(e).__name__] += 1
                    return
                codes[r.status_code] += 1
                if r.status_code == 200:
                    responses[request_id].append(r.json()["ticket_number"])

        await asyncio.gather(*(buy(u, q) for u, q in jobs))
        status = (await client.get("/status")).json()

    return jobs, responses, codes, errors, status


def check(args, jobs, responses, codes, errors, status):
    total, sold, tickets = status["total_tickets"], status["sold"], status["tickets"]
    numbers = [t["ticket_number"] for t in tickets]
    dup_numbers = {n: c for n, c in Counter(numbers).items() if c > 1}
    out_of_range = [n for n in numbers if not 1 <= n <= total]
    users_multi = {u: c for u, c in Counter(t["user_id"] for t in tickets).items() if c > 1}
    inconsistent = {q: ns for q, ns in responses.items() if len(set(ns)) > 1}

    results = {
        "1 no oversell":        (len(tickets) <= total,
                                 f"{len(tickets)} tickets issued for {total} available"),
        "2 no duplicate ticket": (not dup_numbers and not out_of_range,
                                 f"{len(dup_numbers)} ticket numbers issued >1 time "
                                 f"({sum(dup_numbers.values())} rows); {len(out_of_range)} out of range"),
        "3 idempotency":        (not users_multi and not inconsistent,
                                 f"{len(users_multi)} request_ids hold >1 ticket (server rows); "
                                 f"{len(inconsistent)} request_ids told different numbers (responses)"),
        "4 no drift":           (sold == len(tickets),
                                 f"/status sold={sold}, actual rows={len(tickets)}"),
    }

    n_dup_ids = sum(1 for c in Counter(q for _, q in jobs).values() if c > 1)
    print(f"\nrequests={len(jobs)}  concurrency={args.concurrency}  tickets={total}  "
          f"request_ids sent >1 time={n_dup_ids}")
    print(f"HTTP codes: {dict(codes)}   transport errors: {dict(errors) or 0}")
    unexpected = sum(c for code, c in codes.items() if code not in (200, 409)) + sum(errors.values())
    print()
    for name, (ok, detail) in results.items():
        print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name:24} {detail}")

    if unexpected:
        verdict = "INCONCLUSIVE (unexpected errors)"
    else:
        verdict = "PASS" if all(ok for ok, _ in results.values()) else "FAIL"
    print(f"\nOVERALL: {verdict}")
    if args.verbose and dup_numbers:
        print("duplicate ticket numbers (number: rows):", dict(sorted(dup_numbers.items())[:20]))
    return verdict == "PASS"


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--url", default="http://localhost:8000")
    p.add_argument("--tickets", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--requests", type=int, default=1000)
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=200)
    p.add_argument("--dup-fraction", type=float, default=0.2)
    p.add_argument("--dup-copies", type=int, default=2)
    p.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=30.0)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    ok = check(args, *asyncio.run(run(args)))
    raise SystemExit(0 if ok else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Load client v1: stampede the seller, then check the four invariants."""
import argparse
import asyncio
import random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

import httpx


def build_jobs(n_requests, dup_fraction, dup_copies, seed):
    """Return a send order of (user_id, request_id). Duplicate copies sit adjacent
    so they are in flight at the same time (the retry-while-original-pending case)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    jobs, i = [], 0
    while len(jobs) < n_requests:
        user_id, request_id = f"user-{i}", f"req-{i}"
        copies = dup_copies if rng.random() < dup_fraction else 1
        jobs.extend([(user_id, request_id)] * copies)
        i += 1
    return jobs[:n_requests]


async def run(args):
    jobs = build_jobs(args.requests, args.dup_fraction, args.dup_copies, args.seed)
    limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=args.concurrency, max_keepalive_connections=args.concurrency)
    responses = defaultdict(list)          # request_id -> [ticket_number, ...] from 200s
    codes, errors = Counter(), Counter()
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(args.concurrency)

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=args.url, limits=limits, timeout=args.timeout) as client:
        r = await client.post("/reset", json={"tickets": args.tickets})
        r.raise_for_status()

        async def buy(user_id, request_id):
            async with sem:
                try:
                    r = await client.post("/buy", json={"user_id": user_id, "request_id": request_id})
                except httpx.HTTPError as e:
                    errors[type(e).__name__] += 1
                    return
                codes[r.status_code] += 1
                if r.status_code == 200:
                    responses[request_id].append(r.json()["ticket_number"])

        await asyncio.gather(*(buy(u, q) for u, q in jobs))
        status = (await client.get("/status")).json()

    return jobs, responses, codes, errors, status


def check(args, jobs, responses, codes, errors, status):
    total, sold, tickets = status["total_tickets"], status["sold"], status["tickets"]
    numbers = [t["ticket_number"] for t in tickets]
    dup_numbers = {n: c for n, c in Counter(numbers).items() if c > 1}
    out_of_range = [n for n in numbers if not 1 <= n <= total]
    users_multi = {u: c for u, c in Counter(t["user_id"] for t in tickets).items() if c > 1}
    inconsistent = {q: ns for q, ns in responses.items() if len(set(ns)) > 1}

    results = {
        "1 no oversell":        (len(tickets) <= total,
                                 f"{len(tickets)} tickets issued for {total} available"),
        "2 no duplicate ticket": (not dup_numbers and not out_of_range,
                                 f"{len(dup_numbers)} ticket numbers issued >1 time "
                                 f"({sum(dup_numbers.values())} rows); {len(out_of_range)} out of range"),
        "3 idempotency":        (not users_multi and not inconsistent,
                                 f"{len(users_multi)} request_ids hold >1 ticket (server rows); "
                                 f"{len(inconsistent)} request_ids told different numbers (responses)"),
        "4 no drift":           (sold == len(tickets),
                                 f"/status sold={sold}, actual rows={len(tickets)}"),
    }

    n_dup_ids = sum(1 for c in Counter(q for _, q in jobs).values() if c > 1)
    print(f"\nrequests={len(jobs)}  concurrency={args.concurrency}  tickets={total}  "
          f"request_ids sent >1 time={n_dup_ids}")
    print(f"HTTP codes: {dict(codes)}   transport errors: {dict(errors) or 0}")
    unexpected = sum(c for code, c in codes.items() if code not in (200, 409)) + sum(errors.values())
    print()
    for name, (ok, detail) in results.items():
        print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name:24} {detail}")

    if unexpected:
        verdict = "INCONCLUSIVE (unexpected errors)"
    else:
        verdict = "PASS" if all(ok for ok, _ in results.values()) else "FAIL"
    print(f"\nOVERALL: {verdict}")
    if args.verbose and dup_numbers:
        print("duplicate ticket numbers (number: rows):", dict(sorted(dup_numbers.items())[:20]))
    return verdict == "PASS"


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--url", default="http://localhost:8000")
    p.add_argument("--tickets", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--requests", type=int, default=1000)
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=200)
    p.add_argument("--dup-fraction", type=float, default=0.2)
    p.add_argument("--dup-copies", type=int, default=2)
    p.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=30.0)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    ok = check(args, *asyncio.run(run(args)))
    raise SystemExit(0 if ok else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import asyncio
import random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

import httpx


def build_jobs(n_requests, dup_fraction, dup_copies, seed):
    """Return a send order of (user_id, request_id). Duplicate copies sit adjacent
    so they are in flight at the same time (the retry-while-original-pending case)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    jobs, i = [], 0
    while len(jobs) < n_requests:
        user_id, request_id = f"user-{i}", f"req-{i}"
        copies = dup_copies if rng.random() < dup_fraction else 1
        jobs.extend([(user_id, request_id)] * copies)
        i += 1
    return jobs[:n_requests]


async def run(args):
    jobs = build_jobs(args.requests, args.dup_fraction, args.dup_copies, args.seed)
    limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=args.concurrency, max_keepalive_connections=args.concurrency)
    responses = defaultdict(list)          # request_id -> [ticket_number, ...] from 200s
    codes, errors = Counter(), Counter()
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(args.concurrency)

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=args.url, limits=limits, timeout=args.timeout) as client:
        r = await client.post("/reset", json={"tickets": args.tickets})
        r.raise_for_status()

        async def buy(user_id, request_id):
            async with sem:
                try:
                    r = await client.post("/buy", json={"user_id": user_id, "request_id": request_id})
                except httpx.HTTPError as e:
                    errors[type(e).__name__] += 1
                    return
                codes[r.status_code] += 1
                if r.status_code == 200:
                    responses[request_id].append(r.json()["ticket_number"])

        await asyncio.gather(*(buy(u, q) for u, q in jobs))
        status = (await client.get("/status")).json()

    return jobs, responses, codes, errors, status


def check(args, jobs, responses, codes, errors, status):
    total, sold, tickets = status["total_tickets"], status["sold"], status["tickets"]
    numbers = [t["ticket_number"] for t in tickets]
    dup_numbers = {n: c for n, c in Counter(numbers).items() if c > 1}
    out_of_range = [n for n in numbers if not 1 <= n <= total]
    users_multi = {u: c for u, c in Counter(t["user_id"] for t in tickets).items() if c > 1}
    inconsistent = {q: ns for q, ns in responses.items() if len(set(ns)) > 1}

    results = {
        "1 no oversell":        (len(tickets) <= total,
                                 f"{len(tickets)} tickets issued for {total} available"),
        "2 no duplicate ticket": (not dup_numbers and not out_of_range,
                                 f"{len(dup_numbers)} ticket numbers issued >1 time "
                                 f"({sum(dup_numbers.values())} rows); {len(out_of_range)} out of range"),
        "3 idempotency":        (not users_multi and not inconsistent,
                                 f"{len(users_multi)} request_ids hold >1 ticket (server rows); "
                                 f"{len(inconsistent)} request_ids told different numbers (responses)"),
        "4 no drift":           (sold == len(tickets),
                                 f"/status sold={sold}, actual rows={len(tickets)}"),
    }

    n_dup_ids = sum(1 for c in Counter(q for _, q in jobs).values() if c > 1)
    print(f"\nrequests={len(jobs)}  concurrency={args.concurrency}  tickets={total}  "
          f"request_ids sent >1 time={n_dup_ids}")
    print(f"HTTP codes: {dict(codes)}   transport errors: {dict(errors) or 0}")
    unexpected = sum(c for code, c in codes.items() if code not in (200, 409)) + sum(errors.values())
    print()
    for name, (ok, detail) in results.items():
        print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name:24} {detail}")

    if unexpected:
        verdict = "INCONCLUSIVE (unexpected errors)"
    else:
        verdict = "PASS" if all(ok for ok, _ in results.values()) else "FAIL"
    print(f"\nOVERALL: {verdict}")
    if args.verbose and dup_numbers:
        print("duplicate ticket numbers (number: rows):", dict(sorted(dup_numbers.items())[:20]))
    return verdict == "PASS"


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--url", default="http://localhost:8000")
    p.add_argument("--tickets", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--requests", type=int, default=1000)
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=200)
    p.add_argument("--dup-fraction", type=float, default=0.2)
    p.add_argument("--dup-copies", type=int, default=2)
    p.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=30.0)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    jobs, responses, codes, errors, status = asyncio.run(run(args))
    ok = check(args, jobs, responses, codes, errors, status)
    if args.out:
        # Raw evidence: enough to re-derive every verdict without trusting this script's summary.
        with open(args.out, "w") as f:
            json.dump({"args": vars(args), "http_codes": codes, "transport_errors": errors,
                       "responses_by_request_id": responses, "status": status}, f, indent=1)
    raise SystemExit(0 if ok else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Milestone 3 is done: the naive seller broke all four invariants in all 6 runs, with and without the delay. Raw JSON and the text reports are in `results/m3_naive_*`.

| Delay | Tickets issued (of 100) | Duplicate ticket numbers | `/status` said sold | Most rows sharing one ticket number |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50 ms | 466 / 564 / 570 | 80 / 99 / 100 | 100 every time | **10** in every run |
| 0 ms | 160 / 160 / 164 | 41 / 47 / 37 | 100 every time | 5 / 4 / 6 |

**What we learned**
1. **Your pool-size prediction held exactly.** With 50 ms, no ticket number ever had more than 10 rows, and 10 is the pool size. The race window holds as many requests as there are pool connections, not as many as there are clients. With 0 ms the window closes before all 10 line up, so the maximum is 4–6.
2. **"Didn't you add a sleep to make it fail?"** Without the delay it still sold about 60% too many tickets. The delay makes the race worse; it doesn't cause it.
3. **The count drift always undercounts, and the stale counter is what drives the oversell.** `sold` ended at exactly 100 in every run, while the tickets table held 160–570 rows. Sales only stopped once the counter reached the cap.
4. **The two idempotency checks disagreed, which shows why both are needed.** In 50 ms run 1, 37 request_ids had more than one row on the server, but only 5 were given different numbers. When two copies both read `sold=k`, both insert `k+1`, and the buyer hears the same number twice. It looks idempotent from the client side, but there are two rows. **Interview flag:** checking responses alone would have missed most of these.

### Two decisions for you
**A. Should the D12 rule be refined?** Right now any transport error makes a run INCONCLUSIVE, even run 1 with 466 tickets sold for 100. My position: an error can hide a failure but can't create one. A dropped response can't put rows in the database. So the verdict should be:
- any invariant fails → **FAIL**
- all pass, but errors occurred → **INCONCLUSIVE**

This matters more later. When the corrected seller passes under heavy load, errors must still block a PASS. Do you agree?

**B.** Shall I commit this as "M3: naive seller failure evidence (50ms and 0ms, 3 runs each)"? That includes `results/` and the `--out` flag.

### Before Milestone 4: reason it out yourself first
The corrected `/buy` will be one transaction. Before I show any SQL:
1. Postgres's default isolation level is READ COMMITTED. If we just wrap the naive steps in `BEGIN … COMMIT` without adding a lock, **does that fix the oversell?** Why or why not?
2. Which row would you lock with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, and what exactly does that force concurrent `/buy`s to do?
3. With that lock, is `UNIQUE(request_id)` still needed? Think about which two statements the lock is held between, and whether the idempotency check falls inside that window.

"""Load client v1: stampede the seller, then check the four invariants."""
import argparse
import asyncio
import json
import random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

import httpx


def build_jobs(n_requests, dup_fraction, dup_copies, seed):
    """Return a send order of (user_id, request_id). Duplicate copies sit adjacent
    so they are in flight at the same time (the retry-while-original-pending case)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    jobs, i = [], 0
    while len(jobs) < n_requests:
        user_id, request_id = f"user-{i}", f"req-{i}"
        copies = dup_copies if rng.random() < dup_fraction else 1
        jobs.extend([(user_id, request_id)] * copies)
        i += 1
    return jobs[:n_requests]


async def run(args):
    jobs = build_jobs(args.requests, args.dup_fraction, args.dup_copies, args.seed)
    limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=args.concurrency, max_keepalive_connections=args.concurrency)
    responses = defaultdict(list)          # request_id -> [ticket_number, ...] from 200s
    codes, errors = Counter(), Counter()
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(args.concurrency)

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=args.url, limits=limits, timeout=args.timeout) as client:
        r = await client.post("/reset", json={"tickets": args.tickets})
        r.raise_for_status()

        async def buy(user_id, request_id):
            async with sem:
                try:
                    r = await client.post("/buy", json={"user_id": user_id, "request_id": request_id})
                except httpx.HTTPError as e:
                    errors[type(e).__name__] += 1
                    return
                codes[r.status_code] += 1
                if r.status_code == 200:
                    responses[request_id].append(r.json()["ticket_number"])

        await asyncio.gather(*(buy(u, q) for u, q in jobs))
        status = (await client.get("/status")).json()

    return jobs, responses, codes, errors, status


def check(args, jobs, responses, codes, errors, status):
    total, sold, tickets = status["total_tickets"], status["sold"], status["tickets"]
    numbers = [t["ticket_number"] for t in tickets]
    dup_numbers = {n: c for n, c in Counter(numbers).items() if c > 1}
    out_of_range = [n for n in numbers if not 1 <= n <= total]
    users_multi = {u: c for u, c in Counter(t["user_id"] for t in tickets).items() if c > 1}
    inconsistent = {q: ns for q, ns in responses.items() if len(set(ns)) > 1}

    results = {
        "1 no oversell":        (len(tickets) <= total,
                                 f"{len(tickets)} tickets issued for {total} available"),
        "2 no duplicate ticket": (not dup_numbers and not out_of_range,
                                 f"{len(dup_numbers)} ticket numbers issued >1 time "
                                 f"({sum(dup_numbers.values())} rows); {len(out_of_range)} out of range"),
        "3 idempotency":        (not users_multi and not inconsistent,
                                 f"{len(users_multi)} request_ids hold >1 ticket (server rows); "
                                 f"{len(inconsistent)} request_ids told different numbers (responses)"),
        "4 no drift":           (sold == len(tickets),
                                 f"/status sold={sold}, actual rows={len(tickets)}"),
    }

    n_dup_ids = sum(1 for c in Counter(q for _, q in jobs).values() if c > 1)
    print(f"\nrequests={len(jobs)}  concurrency={args.concurrency}  tickets={total}  "
          f"request_ids sent >1 time={n_dup_ids}")
    print(f"HTTP codes: {dict(codes)}   transport errors: {dict(errors) or 0}")
    unexpected = sum(c for code, c in codes.items() if code not in (200, 409)) + sum(errors.values())
    print()
    for name, (ok, detail) in results.items():
        print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name:24} {detail}")

    if unexpected:
        verdict = "INCONCLUSIVE (unexpected errors)"
    else:
        verdict = "PASS" if all(ok for ok, _ in results.values()) else "FAIL"
    print(f"\nOVERALL: {verdict}")
    if args.verbose and dup_numbers:
        print("duplicate ticket numbers (number: rows):", dict(sorted(dup_numbers.items())[:20]))
    return verdict == "PASS"


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--url", default="http://localhost:8000")
    p.add_argument("--tickets", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--requests", type=int, default=1000)
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=200)
    p.add_argument("--dup-fraction", type=float, default=0.2)
    p.add_argument("--dup-copies", type=int, default=2)
    p.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=30.0)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("--out", help="write raw results JSON to this path")
    args = p.parse_args()
    jobs, responses, codes, errors, status = asyncio.run(run(args))
    ok = check(args, jobs, responses, codes, errors, status)
    if args.out:
        # Raw evidence: enough to re-derive every verdict without trusting this script's summary.
        with open(args.out, "w") as f:
            json.dump({"args": vars(args), "http_codes": codes, "transport_errors": errors,
                       "responses_by_request_id": responses, "status": status}, f, indent=1)
    raise SystemExit(0 if ok else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
Milestone 3 is committed as `605bfac`, and it includes the D12 refinement.

## Your answers
1. **Correct.** Under READ COMMITTED, a plain `SELECT` takes no lock and doesn't wait for anyone. Ten transactions can all read `sold=5`, and nothing forces them to take turns.
2. **Correct.** One addition you should be able to state: after a blocked transaction gets the lock, **Postgres re-reads the latest committed version of the row.** So the `sold_count` it sees includes the previous holder's increment. That re-read is what makes `FOR UPDATE` work under READ COMMITTED.
3. **Right conclusion, but the reason needs sharpening, and I'm pushing back on `sale_id`.**
   - **Is UNIQUE needed for correctness?** If the idempotency `SELECT` runs *after* we take the lock, every `/buy` is already serialized. The second copy of a request_id is guaranteed to see the first copy's committed row. So with this flow, UNIQUE is **defense in depth, not the mechanism.** It turns "the app forgot to check" or "someone later moved the check before the lock" from silent corruption into a loud error. Say it that way in the interview; don't claim both layers are needed.
   - **Drop `sale_id`.** We have exactly one sale, and `/reset` wipes everything. A `sale_id` column solves a multi-event problem we don't have (rule 5). If the interviewer adds "support multiple concurrent sales", adding it then is a two-minute change, and a good one to make live.

## Corrected transaction flow
```
BEGIN                                                        -- READ COMMITTED (default)
 1. SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE
      └─ every other /buy blocks here until we COMMIT/ROLLBACK
 2. SELECT ticket_number FROM tickets WHERE request_id = $rid
      └─ found → COMMIT, return 200 {ticket_number}           (replay: same ticket)
 3. if sold_count >= total_tickets → COMMIT, return 409 {sold_out: true}
 4. INSERT INTO tickets (ticket_number, user_id, request_id) VALUES (sold_count + 1, ...)
 5. UPDATE sale SET sold_count = sold_count + 1 WHERE id = 1
COMMIT                                                       -- lock released; insert + counter visible together
any exception → ROLLBACK (asyncpg's `async with conn.transaction()`)
```

**Statement order is critical. This is the biggest interview flag in the project.** Step 2 must come *after* step 1. Under READ COMMITTED each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so step 2 runs after we hold the lock and sees everything the previous lock holder committed. Put the idempotency check before the lock and you're back to check-then-act. That's the bug UNIQUE would then catch, and it's why UNIQUE earns its place.

**Invariant 4 (no drift) is guaranteed atomically, not structurally.** The insert and the counter update commit together or not at all. But no plain constraint can express `sold_count = COUNT(tickets)`. Be honest about that: invariants 1–3 have constraint backstops, and invariant 4 relies on the transaction. Enforcing it in the schema would need a trigger, or dropping the counter.

## Constrained schema
```sql
sale(id INT PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1),
     total_tickets INT NOT NULL CHECK (total_tickets >= 0),
     sold_count    INT NOT NULL CHECK (sold_count BETWEEN 0 AND total_tickets))  -- oversell backstop
tickets(ticket_number INT PRIMARY KEY CHECK (ticket_number >= 1),               -- inv 2 backstop
        user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
        request_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE)                                         -- inv 3 backstop
```

**`/status` fix:** read the sale row and the tickets in one `REPEATABLE READ` read-only transaction, so both reads come from the **same snapshot**. Otherwise a mid-sale `/status` could land between two commits and show `sold` and the rows disagreeing, which would be false drift. The buyer only reads status after the storm, so it wouldn't catch this, but the spec says "always".

## Alternative I'm recommending against, for now
**Pre-create tickets 1…N and claim one with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.** This makes oversell *structurally* impossible, because there are only N rows. It also lets buyers claim different tickets in parallel instead of queueing on one hot row. Two costs: idempotency and the counter become harder, and it optimizes a bottleneck we **haven't measured yet**. The single locked row almost certainly caps throughput, and Milestone 7 should *show* that with `pg_locks`. If it does, this becomes the evidence-backed fix. Logged as a Milestone 7 candidate.

## Decisions I need from you (Milestone 4 touches several files)
**1. What happens to the naive code?**
- **(a) Recommended:** `SELLER_MODE=naive|safe` environment variable. Both `/buy` functions live in `app.py`, and each mode has its own schema file. The before/after comparison can be reproduced from one checkout with one variable, which the README needs. Cost: about 30 lines of intentionally wrong code stay in the repo, clearly labelled.
- **(b)** Replace the naive code entirely, and the failure is reproducible only by checking out tag `m3`. Less code, but a clean-checkout reviewer can't rerun the "before" run easily.

**2. The same `request_id` sent with a different `user_id`.** This question has been open since Milestone 1, and the idempotency check now has to answer it.
- **(a) Recommended:** return `422 {"error": "request_id reused with different user_id"}`. That's how Stripe treats reused idempotency keys with a different payload. Silently giving alice's ticket to bob would be wrong.
- **(b)** Return the existing ticket regardless. Simpler, but it leaks another user's ticket.

**Files:** `seller/app.py` (safe `/buy`, snapshot `/status`, mode switch), new `seller/schema_safe.sql`, `docker-compose.yml` (pass `SELLER_MODE`), and `DECISIONS_LOG.md`. Once they're in, I'll run the Milestone 3 workload against it: 50 ms and 0 ms, 3 runs each, same seeds. Approve 1 and 2 and I'll write it.

import asyncio
import os
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

DATABASE_URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]
DB_POOL_SIZE = int(os.environ.get("DB_POOL_SIZE", "10"))
NAIVE_DELAY_MS = int(os.environ.get("NAIVE_DELAY_MS", "50"))
SCHEMA = (Path(__file__).parent / "schema_naive.sql").read_text()

app = FastAPI()
pool: asyncpg.Pool


@app.on_event("startup")
async def startup():
    global pool
    pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(DATABASE_URL, min_size=DB_POOL_SIZE, max_size=DB_POOL_SIZE)


class ResetRequest(BaseModel):
    tickets: int


class BuyRequest(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    request_id: str


@app.post("/reset")
async def reset(body: ResetRequest):
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        await conn.execute(SCHEMA)
        await conn.execute("INSERT INTO sale (total_tickets, sold_count) VALUES ($1, 0)", body.tickets)
    return {"total_tickets": body.tickets}


@app.post("/buy")
async def buy(body: BuyRequest):
    # NAIVE: no transaction, no lock. Each statement autocommits on its own,
    # so other requests can interleave between every step below.
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        # 1. Idempotency check (check-then-act: two copies can both see "not found").
        existing = await conn.fetchval(
            "SELECT ticket_number FROM tickets WHERE request_id = $1", body.request_id
        )
        if existing is not None:
            return {"ticket_number": existing}

        # 2. Capacity check (check-then-act: many readers can see the same sold_count).
        sale = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale")
        sold = sale["sold_count"]
        if sold >= sale["total_tickets"]:
            return JSONResponse(status_code=409, content={"sold_out": True})

        # 3. Simulated work between check and act; widens the race window.
        await asyncio.sleep(NAIVE_DELAY_MS / 1000)

        # 4. Ticket number derived from the stale read -> duplicate numbers.
        ticket_number = sold + 1
        await conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO tickets (ticket_number, user_id, request_id) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
            ticket_number, body.user_id, body.request_id,
        )

        # 5. Read-modify-write computed in Python -> lost updates -> sold_count drifts.
        await conn.execute("UPDATE sale SET sold_count = $1", sold + 1)

    return {"ticket_number": ticket_number}


@app.get("/status")
async def status():
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        sale = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale")
        rows = await conn.fetch("SELECT ticket_number, user_id FROM tickets ORDER BY ticket_number")
    return {
        "total_tickets": sale["total_tickets"] if sale else 0,
        "sold": sale["sold_count"] if sale else 0,
        # A list, not a dict: duplicate ticket numbers must stay visible.
        "tickets": [{"ticket_number": r["ticket_number"], "user_id": r["user_id"]} for r in rows],
    }

# Decision log (running — becomes DECISIONS.md)

| # | Decision | Status | Rationale / evidence | Still uncertain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D0 | Project has its own git repo | done | Parent repo was rooted at home dir (exposed .ssh/.aws) | — |
| D1 | Shared state + correctness in Postgres, not an in-process lock | accepted | Process lock protects one process's memory only | Evidence due in multi-instance stretch (M8) |
| D2 | Naive race window is configurable (`NAIVE_DELAY_MS`, default 50); 0 ms run also reported | accepted | Delay stands in for real work between check and act; the 0 ms run answers "did you rig it?" | Whether 0 ms still reproduces the failure — to measure in M3 |
| D3 | asyncpg + raw SQL | accepted | Transaction boundaries and locks visible line by line | — |
| D4 | Naive seller keeps a separate `sold_count`, updated by Python-side read-modify-write | accepted | `COUNT(*)` cannot drift by definition; a stored counter with lost updates can, so the naive run can show drift. Corrected version must update it atomically with the insert | — |
| D5 | `/status.tickets` is a list of `{ticket_number, user_id}` | accepted | JSON object keys are unique; duplicate ticket numbers would be silently collapsed | — |
| D6 | Sold out → HTTP 409 `{"sold_out": true}` | accepted | — | — |
| D7 | `/reset` drops and recreates tables from the schema file | accepted | Schema changes (naive → constrained) apply on reset with no stale volume; reset is never under load | — |
| D8 | Single uvicorn worker | accepted | Multiple workers = multiple processes = the multi-instance problem, deliberately deferred | — |
| D9 | Buyer: semaphore-capped concurrency, httpx connection limits set to match | accepted | httpx defaults to 100 max connections; would silently cap concurrency and measure the client, not the server | Client-side limits at high concurrency (M7) |
| D10 | Duplicate copies sent adjacent (in flight together) | accepted | The retry-while-original-pending case is the hard one; a sequential replay passes even the naive seller | Sequential replay not separately reported |
| D11 | Idempotency checked twice: server rows (one user_id ↔ one request_id, so a user with >1 row = violation) and client responses (copies told different numbers) | accepted | Independent sources; one catches stored duplicates, the other catches contradictory answers | — |
| D12 | Verdict: any invariant fails → FAIL; all pass but non-200/409 or transport errors → INCONCLUSIVE; PASS only if clean | accepted (revised after M3) | Errors can hide a violation but cannot create one (violations measured from server rows). Original rule marked a 466-for-100 run "inconclusive", which was wrong | — |

## Observations
- **M1 smoke test (sequential):** naive seller is correct with no concurrency: replayed `r1` got the same ticket, sold out at 2, `sold` matched rows. The bug only exists under interleaving, so a concurrent client is the only way to expose it.

- **M2 checker false-positive test:** `--requests 150 --tickets 100 --concurrency 1` against naive seller → all PASS; 119×200 + 31×409 matches expected accounting exactly (126 unique ids, 24 replayed). Checker's ability to catch failures (true positives) is proven in M3.
- **Prediction recorded before M3** (the user's own): oversell + duplicate numbers (many readers see same count), drift (lost update), idempotency failure for concurrent same-request_id copies. Magnitude: unknown, to be measured.

- **M3 naive failure runs** (1000 req, 100 tickets, concurrency 200, 20% dup, pool 10; raw JSON + reports in `results/m3_naive_*`):

  | delay | run | rows issued | dup numbers | request_ids with >1 row (server) / told different numbers (client) | /status sold | max rows per number |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 50ms | 1 | 466 | 80 | 37 / 5 | 100 | 10 |
  | 50ms | 2 | 564 | 99 | 9 / 1 | 100 | 10 |
  | 50ms | 3 | 570 | 100 | 9 / 3 | 100 | 10 |
  | 0ms | 1 | 160 | 41 | 3 / 1 | 100 | 5 |
  | 0ms | 2 | 160 | 47 | 1 / 1 | 100 | 4 |
  | 0ms | 3 | 164 | 37 | 2 / 0 | 100 | 6 |

  - All four invariants failed in all 6 runs. 50ms run 1 is formally INCONCLUSIVE (1 `ReadError`), but its failures are measured from server rows (see D12 revision question).
  - **Pool-size prediction confirmed:** max rows for a single ticket number is exactly 10 = `DB_POOL_SIZE` in every 50ms run, never more. With 0ms the window closes before all 10 align (max 4–6).
  - **The delay only amplifies the race:** 0ms still oversells about 60% (160–164 rows for 100 tickets). Answer to "did you rig it?"
  - **Drift is always an under-count, and the counter is what stops the oversell:** `sold` ended at exactly 100 in all runs; rows kept being inserted until the lost-update counter finally reached the cap. Oversell ≈ average number of writers per counter increment.
  - **The two idempotency checks disagree, and that is informative:** e.g. 37 server-side vs 5 client-side. Two concurrent copies both read `sold=k`, both insert `k+1`, and the client hears the *same* number twice — looks idempotent from the client, but two rows exist. The server-row check (D11a) catches what the response check cannot.

## Open questions / to revisit
- `ReadError` in 50ms run 1: seller logged no errors and no non-200/409, so the failure was at the connection level (suspect: Docker Desktop port proxy on Windows). Unproven. Watch whether it recurs under higher load (M7).
- DB pool size (`DB_POOL_SIZE=10`) caps how many requests are inside the race window at once. The concurrency the DB sees is the pool size, not the client count. Matters for M3 and M7.
- `/status` does two separate reads (sale row, then tickets): not a consistent snapshot. Fine for naive; decide for the corrected seller.
- Same `request_id` sent with a *different* `user_id`: what should happen? Not yet decided.

## Interview flags
- Naive lost-update feedback loop: `sold_count` drifts low → the capacity check passes for more buyers → oversell gets worse.
- "Didn't you just add a sleep to make it break?" → answer with the 0 ms run data.

That's a property of this particular code, not a guarantee. A crash between the insert and the update would still cause drift.

If that's what happens, it's the evidence you want: **the constraints keep the data correct but break the service, while the lock keeps both correct.** That's what "primary mechanism vs defense in depth" means in practice.

import asyncio
import os
from pathlib import Path

import asyncpg
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

DATABASE_URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]
DB_POOL_SIZE = int(os.environ.get("DB_POOL_SIZE", "10"))
# Simulated work between the capacity check and the insert, applied in BOTH modes
# at the same point so naive-vs-safe is a fair comparison.
WORK_DELAY_MS = int(os.environ.get("WORK_DELAY_MS", "50"))
SELLER_MODE = os.environ.get("SELLER_MODE", "safe")
if SELLER_MODE not in ("naive", "safe"):
    raise ValueError(f"SELLER_MODE must be naive or safe, got {SELLER_MODE!r}")
SCHEMA = (Path(__file__).parent / f"schema_{SELLER_MODE}.sql").read_text()

app = FastAPI()
pool: asyncpg.Pool


@app.on_event("startup")
async def startup():
    global pool
    pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(DATABASE_URL, min_size=DB_POOL_SIZE, max_size=DB_POOL_SIZE)


class ResetRequest(BaseModel):
    tickets: int


class BuyRequest(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    request_id: str


@app.post("/reset")
async def reset(body: ResetRequest):
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        await conn.execute(SCHEMA)
        await conn.execute("INSERT INTO sale (total_tickets, sold_count) VALUES ($1, 0)", body.tickets)
    return {"total_tickets": body.tickets}


@app.post("/buy")
async def buy(body: BuyRequest):
    return await (buy_safe(body) if SELLER_MODE == "safe" else buy_naive(body))


async def buy_safe(body: BuyRequest):
    # One transaction (READ COMMITTED). Statement ORDER matters: the idempotency
    # check must come after the lock, so it sees every previously committed sale.
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        async with conn.transaction():
            # 1. Lock the sale row. Every other /buy blocks here until we commit.
            #    On acquiring the lock, Postgres re-reads the latest committed row.
            sale = await conn.fetchrow(
                "SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE"
            )

            # 2. Idempotency: under the lock, so no concurrent copy can slip past.
            existing = await conn.fetchrow(
                "SELECT ticket_number, user_id FROM tickets WHERE request_id = $1", body.request_id
            )
            if existing is not None:
                if existing["user_id"] != body.user_id:
                    return JSONResponse(status_code=422, content={
                        "error": "request_id was already used by a different user_id"})
                return {"ticket_number": existing["ticket_number"]}

            # 3. Capacity.
            if sale["sold_count"] >= sale["total_tickets"]:
                return JSONResponse(status_code=409, content={"sold_out": True})

            # Same simulated work as naive mode, but here it is done while holding the lock.
            await asyncio.sleep(WORK_DELAY_MS / 1000)

            # 4 + 5. Insert and count commit together or not at all (invariant 4).
            ticket_number = sale["sold_count"] + 1
            await conn.execute(
                "INSERT INTO tickets (ticket_number, user_id, request_id) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
                ticket_number, body.user_id, body.request_id,
            )
            await conn.execute("UPDATE sale SET sold_count = sold_count + 1 WHERE id = 1")
    return {"ticket_number": ticket_number}


async def buy_naive(body: BuyRequest):
    # NAIVE: no transaction, no lock. Each statement autocommits on its own,
    # so other requests can interleave between every step below.
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        # 1. Idempotency check (check-then-act: two copies can both see "not found").
        existing = await conn.fetchval(
            "SELECT ticket_number FROM tickets WHERE request_id = $1", body.request_id
        )
        if existing is not None:
            return {"ticket_number": existing}

        # 2. Capacity check (check-then-act: many readers can see the same sold_count).
        sale = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale")
        sold = sale["sold_count"]
        if sold >= sale["total_tickets"]:
            return JSONResponse(status_code=409, content={"sold_out": True})

        # 3. Simulated work between check and act; widens the race window.
        await asyncio.sleep(WORK_DELAY_MS / 1000)

        # 4. Ticket number derived from the stale read -> duplicate numbers.
        ticket_number = sold + 1
        await conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO tickets (ticket_number, user_id, request_id) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
            ticket_number, body.user_id, body.request_id,
        )

        # 5. Read-modify-write computed in Python -> lost updates -> sold_count drifts.
        await conn.execute("UPDATE sale SET sold_count = $1", sold + 1)

    return {"ticket_number": ticket_number}


@app.get("/status")
async def status():
    # One REPEATABLE READ snapshot: both reads see the same set of commits, so a
    # mid-sale /status cannot show sold and rows from different moments.
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        async with conn.transaction(isolation="repeatable_read", readonly=True):
            sale = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT total_tickets, sold_count FROM sale")
            rows = await conn.fetch("SELECT ticket_number, user_id FROM tickets ORDER BY ticket_number")
    return {
        "total_tickets": sale["total_tickets"] if sale else 0,
        "sold": sale["sold_count"] if sale else 0,
        # A list, not a dict: duplicate ticket numbers must stay visible.
        "tickets": [{"ticket_number": r["ticket_number"], "user_id": r["user_id"]} for r in rows],
    }

The lock (M4 safe runs) keeps data correct **and** gives every buyer a clean 200/409. That is the evidence for "lock = primary mechanism, constraints = defense in depth".
  - Every 500 matched a `tickets_pkey` violation 1:1 in the seller log.
  - **Surprise: `request_id` UNIQUE never fired.** Concurrent copies read the same `sold`, so they collide on ticket_number too; Postgres aborts on the first unique index it checks (the PK). UNIQUE(request_id) would fire alone only if copies read *different* counts — possible, not observed. Its independent value is therefore argued, not demonstrated.

  - **Implied rejected alternative — optimistic concurrency (constraints + catch-and-retry, no lock):** ~7.3–7.8 conflicts per successful sale at this contention. Each retry re-reads and re-contends, so under a stampede it trades lock waiting for wasted round-trips. Pessimistic row lock chosen for the high-contention case; not benchmarked head-to-head.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| D0 | Project has its own git repo | done | Parent repo was rooted at home dir (exposed .ssh/.aws) | — |
| D1 | Shared state + correctness in Postgres, not an in-process lock | accepted | Process lock protects one process's memory only | Evidence due in multi-instance stretch (M8) |
| D2 | Naive race window is configurable (`NAIVE_DELAY_MS`, default 50); 0 ms run also reported | accepted | Delay stands in for real work between check and act; the 0 ms run answers "did you rig it?" | Whether 0 ms still reproduces the failure — to measure in M3 |
| D3 | asyncpg + raw SQL | accepted | Transaction boundaries and locks visible line by line | — |
| D4 | Naive seller keeps a separate `sold_count`, updated by Python-side read-modify-write | accepted | `COUNT(*)` cannot drift by definition; a stored counter with lost updates can, so the naive run can show drift. Corrected version must update it atomically with the insert | — |
| D5 | `/status.tickets` is a list of `{ticket_number, user_id}` | accepted | JSON object keys are unique; duplicate ticket numbers would be silently collapsed | — |
| D6 | Sold out → HTTP 409 `{"sold_out": true}` | accepted | — | — |
| D7 | `/reset` drops and recreates tables from the schema file | accepted | Schema changes (naive → constrained) apply on reset with no stale volume; reset is never under load | — |
| D8 | Single uvicorn worker | accepted | Multiple workers = multiple processes = the multi-instance problem, deliberately deferred | — |
| D9 | Buyer: semaphore-capped concurrency, httpx connection limits set to match | accepted | httpx defaults to 100 max connections; would silently cap concurrency and measure the client, not the server | Client-side limits at high concurrency (M7) |
| D10 | Duplicate copies sent adjacent (in flight together) | accepted | The retry-while-original-pending case is the hard one; a sequential replay passes even the naive seller | Sequential replay not separately reported |
| D11 | Idempotency checked twice: server rows (one user_id ↔ one request_id, so a user with >1 row = violation) and client responses (copies told different numbers) | accepted | Independent sources; one catches stored duplicates, the other catches contradictory answers | — |
| D13 | Safe `/buy`: one READ COMMITTED txn — `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` sale row → idempotency check → capacity → insert → `sold_count = sold_count + 1` → commit | accepted | Lock serializes check+act; after acquiring it Postgres re-reads the latest committed row; idempotency check sits *after* the lock so it sees all prior commits. Evidence: M4 runs below | Throughput cost of one hot row (M7) |
| D14 | Constraints: `sale.sold_count BETWEEN 0 AND total`, `tickets.ticket_number` PK, `request_id` UNIQUE, single sale row `CHECK (id=1)` | accepted | Backstops for invariants 1–3 — defense in depth, NOT the mechanism (the lock is). Invariant 4 has no constraint backstop; it relies on insert + counter in one txn | Backstops never fired in M4 — not yet demonstrated |
| D15 | No `sale_id` | accepted (pushback) | Single sale, `/reset` wipes all; multi-sale is a problem we don't have | Easy live change if asked |

| D17 | Same request_id + different user_id → 422 | accepted | Stripe-style: reused key with different payload is a client error; returning the ticket would leak it to another user. Verified by curl | — |

Original rule marked a 466-for-100 run "inconclusive", which was wrong | — |

## Observations
- **M1 smoke test (sequential):** naive seller is correct with no concurrency: replayed `r1` got the same ticket, sold out at 2, `sold` matched rows. The bug only exists under interleaving, so a concurrent client is the only way to expose it.

- **M2 checker false-positive test:** `--requests 150 --tickets 100 --concurrency 1` against naive seller → all PASS; 119×200 + 31×409 matches expected accounting exactly (126 unique ids, 24 replayed). Checker's ability to catch failures (true positives) is proven in M3.
- **Prediction recorded before M3** (the user's own): oversell + duplicate numbers (many readers see same count), drift (lost update), idempotency failure for concurrent same-request_id copies. Magnitude: unknown, to be measured.

- **M3 naive failure runs** (1000 req, 100 tickets, concurrency 200, 20% dup, pool 10; raw JSON + reports in `results/m3_naive_*`):

  | delay | run | rows issued | dup numbers | request_ids with >1 row (server) / told different numbers (client) | /status sold | max rows per number |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 50ms | 1 | 466 | 80 | 37 / 5 | 100 | 10 |
  | 50ms | 2 | 564 | 99 | 9 / 1 | 100 | 10 |
  | 50ms | 3 | 570 | 100 | 9 / 3 | 100 | 10 |
  | 0ms | 1 | 160 | 41 | 3 / 1 | 100 | 5 |
  | 0ms | 2 | 160 | 47 | 1 / 1 | 100 | 4 |
  | 0ms | 3 | 164 | 37 | 2 / 0 | 100 | 6 |

  - All four invariants failed in all 6 runs. 50ms run 1 is formally INCONCLUSIVE (1 `ReadError`), but its failures are measured from server rows (see D12 revision question).
  - **Pool-size prediction confirmed:** max rows for a single ticket number is exactly 10 = `DB_POOL_SIZE` in every 50ms run, never more. With 0ms the window closes before all 10 align (max 4–6).
  - **The delay only amplifies the race:** 0ms still oversells about 60% (160–164 rows for 100 tickets). Answer to "did you rig it?"
  - **Drift is always an under-count, and the counter is what stops the oversell:** `sold` ended at exactly 100 in all runs; rows kept being inserted until the lost-update counter finally reached the cap. Oversell ≈ average number of writers per counter increment.
  - **The two idempotency checks disagree, and that is informative:** e.g. 37 server-side vs 5 client-side. Two concurrent copies both read `sold=k`, both insert `k+1`, and the client hears the *same* number twice — looks idempotent from the client, but two rows exist. The server-row check (D11a) catches what the response check cannot.

- **M4 naive regression after refactor:** 493 rows for 100 (in M3 range 466–570) → refactor preserved naive behavior. `results/m4_naive_regression_50ms.*`
- **M4 safe runs** (same workload + seeds as M3; `results/m4_safe_*`):

  | delay | run | rows | dup numbers | idempotency (server/client) | sold | verdict | wall time |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 50ms | 1 | 100 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 100 | PASS | 24.3s |
  | 50ms | 2 | 100 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 100 | PASS | 27.2s |
  | 50ms | 3 | 100 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 100 | INCONCLUSIVE (1 ReadError) | 28.2s |
  | 0ms | 1 | 100 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 100 | PASS | 15.5s |
  | 0ms | 2 | 100 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 100 | PASS | 14.1s |
  | 0ms | 3 | 100 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 100 | PASS | 11.4s |

  - Invariants held in 6/6 runs. The 200 count above 100 (116–124) = replays of winning request_ids getting their original ticket back (response check confirms same number).
  - Second `ReadError` (now 2 across 13 concurrent runs). Revised D12 correctly refused to call it PASS.
  - **Unexplained slowness:** 0ms safe still takes 11–15s for 1000 requests (~70–90 req/s). Serialized 100 × 50ms only explains ~5s of the 50ms runs. Not investigated — M7. Hypotheses, unverified: sold-out requests still queue on the lock; Docker Desktop networking; client overhead.

## Open questions / to revisit
- `ReadError` in 50ms run 1: seller logged no errors and no non-200/409, so the failure was at the connection level (suspect: Docker Desktop port proxy on Windows). Unproven. Watch whether it recurs under higher load (M7).
- DB pool size (`DB_POOL_SIZE=10`) caps how many requests are inside the race window at once. The concurrency the DB sees is the pool size, not the client count. Matters for M3 and M7.
- `/status` does two separate reads (sale row, then tickets): not a consistent snapshot. Fine for naive; decide for the corrected seller.
- Same `request_id` sent with a *different* `user_id`: what should happen? Not yet decided.

## Interview flags
- Naive lost-update feedback loop: `sold_count` drifts low → the capacity check passes for more buyers → oversell gets worse.
- "Didn't you just add a sleep to make it break?" → answer with the 0 ms run data.

The constraint test backs up the claim, and Milestone 4 is committed as `f598946`.

**Result:** I ran the racy naive code against the safe schema, with the same workload and seeds as before.

| Setup | Tickets issued (of 100) | Buyers who got an HTTP 500 |
|---|---|---|
| Naive code, no constraints (Milestone 3) | 466–570 | 0 |
| **Naive code + constraints** | **100** | **73–78%** |
| Safe code (lock + constraints) | 100 | 0 |

- **The constraints alone keep the data correct but break the service.** Every 500 lined up one-to-one with a primary-key violation on `tickets.ticket_number` in the seller log. The lock gives correct data *and* a clean 200 or 409 for every buyer. That's the evidence for "the lock is the primary mechanism, the constraints are defense in depth."
- **The UNIQUE constraint on `request_id` never fired.** Two copies of the same request read the same count, so they collide on ticket number too, and Postgres rejects on the primary key first. So its separate value is still an argument, not something we've shown. If you're asked "have you ever seen that constraint catch something?", the honest answer is not yet.
- **This also argues against the optimistic alternative** (no lock, catch the conflict and retry). At this contention there were about 7–8 failed attempts per successful sale. We haven't benchmarked the two side by side, so treat this as reasoning backed by one measurement.
- **The "no drift" invariant held**, but because of how this particular code runs, not because any constraint enforces it.

The change was a small `SELLER_SCHEMA` override in [seller/app.py](seller/app.py) and [docker-compose.yml](docker-compose.yml); it's only used for this experiment. - The `ReadError` (2 in 13 runs, cause unknown).
- The 11–15 second run time for 1,000 requests, which we're leaving for Milestone 7.
- `/status` giving a consistent answer during a sale is designed in but hasn't been tested.

**Next is Milestone 6, load client v2.** A question to think about before we plan it: the buyer records every 200 response and every ticket in `/status`. **Which failure could only be caught by comparing the two, and why would neither side notice it alone?**
